content: The evidence regarding the impact of mass drug administration (MDA) on all-cause hospitalizations within 0–1 months post-MDA is uncertain due to significant imprecision and bias. Data from one observational study (non-randomized) showed that changes in hospital admissions due to severe malaria ranged from a 31% decrease to an 8% increase during the first four weeks after the initial round of MDA, and from a 19% decrease to an 8% increase during the four weeks following the second round of MDA. Statistically significant changes were observed at three of eight time points. However, due to the lack of data on sample population sizes and non-MDA control areas, absolute effects could not be calculated. The evidence on whether MDA increases or decreases severe malaria hospitalizations within 0–1 months post-MDA is also uncertain due to serious risk of bias and imprecision. Parasitologically confirmed malaria cases showed reductions ranging from 35% to 62% during the first four weeks after the first round of MDA, and from 26% to 58% during the four weeks after the second round. These reductions were statistically significant compared to baseline. However, similar reductions were observed in non-MDA control areas, and the confidence intervals for both MDA and non-MDA groups overlapped at all but two time points immediately after the first round of MDA. Absolute effects could not be calculated due to the lack of data on sample sizes. The systematic review identified eight cluster-randomized controlled trials (cRCTs) conducted in very low to low transmission settings across six countries (Cambodia, Lao People’s Democratic Republic, Myanmar, United Republic of Tanzania, Viet Nam, and Zambia). Most studies conducted three rounds of MDA within one year, while others conducted one, two, or four rounds over varying timeframes. Meta-analyses showed reductions in the prevalence and incidence of Plasmodium falciparum infection 1–3 months after the last round of MDA, but no significant impact on clinical malaria. Longer-term evaluations showed either no impact or very low-certainty evidence. Adverse events were infrequently measured, complicating interpretation, but reported rates of adverse events and serious adverse events were low. Only one study measured markers of artemisinin resistance and found no evidence of increased drug-resistant parasites. In moderate to high transmission settings, the review identified two cRCTs and two non-randomized studies (NRSs) conducted in four countries (Burkina Faso, Gambia, Nigeria, and Zambia). Among the cRCTs, one study conducted four rounds of MDA with dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine (DP) over 15 months, while the other conducted one round with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine plus artesunate (SP+AS). The NRSs involved nine rounds of sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine every 10 weeks over 18 months or multiple rounds of chloroquine or amodiaquine combined with low-dose primaquine every 14 days. Meta-analyses of cRCTs showed little to no effect of MDA on P. falciparum prevalence, incidence, or clinical malaria across all time points, with lowto moderate-certainty evidence. NRSs suggested a slight impact on P. falciparum prevalence at 4–12 and 12–24 months, with low-certainty evidence. Only one cRCT measured adverse events, finding a small increase in the MDA arm, but the evidence was of very low certainty. None of the studies measured drug resistance markers. The certainty of evidence for MDA’s impact on malaria outcomes is limited by serious risks of bias, imprecision, and inconsistency across studies. Confidence intervals often included both no effect and substantial effects, and small event numbers frequently failed to meet optimal information size. Additionally, the lack of data on adverse events, serious adverse events, and drug resistance markers in control groups further limits the interpretability of findings.
